papers.title: DREAM - Deliberative Replay, Evaluation, Abstraction and Memory: Evidence-Governed Counterfactual Consolidation for Persistent AI Agents
Learning to remember: advances in memory mechanisms for large language models
papers.summary: Abstract Memory has become a central mechanism for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond fixed context windows, stateless interaction, and static parametric knowledge. This survey organizes the literature around three complementary dimensions: the life cycle of memory, the storage substrate, and the system role that memory plays in LLM-based agents, while using cognitive-science-inspired memory concepts as a lightweight conceptual motivation rather than as a separate technical contribution or implementation family. On this basis, we distinguish three mechanism families: nonparametric memory, where information is stored outside model parameters in text, graph, multimodal, or database-like structures; parametric memory, where information is stored or accessed through activations, key-value caches, learned modules, adapter-based parameterizations, or model weights; and memory for agent evolution, where stored experiences support reinforcement learning, continual learning, procedural reuse, context engineering, and agent harness design. Evaluation is treated as a separate cross-cutting component rather than as a memory mechanism. Unlike surveys that focus primarily on retrieval-augmented generation or long-context modeling, this paper emphasizes the full memory life cycle: construction, maintenance, retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, governance, and evaluation. papers.title: Cross-Session Internet Task Continuity: Maintaining Autonomous Task State Across Disconnected Interactions and Digital Environments
papers.summary: The increasing development of generative artificial intelligence, autonomous agents, and intent-driven Internet systems is creating opportunities for digital systems to undertake complex tasks that extend beyond individual interactions. Many Internet tasks require multiple execution stages, interactions with heterogeneous digital services, information collection, decision-making, and subsequent verification. However, conventional conversational and task-oriented systems frequently organize execution around individual sessions or temporary interaction contexts. When a session ends, an execution environment becomes unavailable, or a user returns through a different interface, previously accumulated task progress may not be directly accessible or operationally recoverable. Consequently, systems may need to reconstruct previous activities, repeat completed operations, rediscover relevant information, or request that users provide previously established context. This paper proposes Cross-Session Internet Task Continuity (CSITC), a conceptual framework for maintaining autonomous Internet task execution across disconnected interactions and digital environments. Rather than treating historical conversations as the primary unit of persistence, CSITC treats the task execution state as an independently maintainable computational object. papers.title: Evidence constrained agentic retrieval augmented generation for substation civil engineering preliminary design documents in a single project study
papers.summary: Abstract Substation civil engineering preliminary design documents must integrate project-specific conditions, current regulatory requirements, typical design practices, and historical engineering experience while maintaining consistency across architectural, structural, general-layout, foundation, road, drainage, and technical-indicator sections. Conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems remain vulnerable to condition-insensitive retrieval, unequal source authority, incompatible evidence, unsupported engineering claims, and parameter drift during long-document drafting. This study proposes an Evidence-Constrained Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, termed EC-ARAG. The framework combines regulation-aware evidence representation, validity-gated hybrid retrieval, source-role-aware conflict resolution, dual planning--retrieval and generation--verification--repair loops, and global project-state memory. The experimental corpus comprised 36 national and industry standards, 12 enterprise standards, 18 typical-design documents, 64 historical preliminary design documents, and nine project-input documents. The held-out evaluation included 120 retrieval queries, 80 applicability cases, 48 evidence-conflict cases, 318 atomic design propositions, and five independent generation runs. papers.title: Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
papers.summary: Enterprise AI agents increasingly split a user's request across subagents and merge their results, and each handoff can summarize away, alter or ignore a requirement. We report a preregistered study with synthetic, exactly scorable tasks comparing free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs the manifest with HMAC-SHA256, and deterministic code verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no net loss of conformant commits relative to structured handoffs. Signing is what defeats in-transit tampering: an unsigned manifest committed violations in 79% of mutated runs, the signed one in none. On identical trajectories the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, with 7% versus 50% false alarms. An oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits: the residual risk comes from extraction errors made before signing. A preregistered pre-signing injection attack confirmed this boundary: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest violations from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 8.3% to 75.0% (GPT-5.6-luna), and the signature then authenticated t

papers.title: All Permissions Granted: Agentic AI, Delegated Access, and the Governance of Semantic Footprints
papers.summary: This review examines how agentic AI reorganizes privacy, accountability and user agency by turning delegated access into operational context. Agentic AI is treated as a graded socio-technical configuration rather than a clean rupture with conversational AI: conversational interfaces may be coupled with contextual retrieval and memory, external tools and applications, organizational data, and execution or delegated action. The review synthesizes public documentation from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, GitHub, DeepSeek and the Model Context Protocol ecosystem, alongside governance and cybersecurity frameworks and scholarship in human-AI interaction, privacy, infrastructure, accountability and usable security. Its contribution is to clarify how user content, communication and scheduling records, repository and browser context, and persistent traces such as logs, feedback, memories and local execution records can become semantic footprints when they reveal priorities, dependencies, intentions, vulnerabilities, roles or possible actions within agentic processes. The review develops the concepts of delegated temporal compression, capability amplification, semantic footprints, the agentic permission grey box and dynamic trust boundaries. Formal consent is insufficient when AI systems operate across fragmented informational environments. Users and organizations require capacity

papers.title: vibyverse: an integrated computational chemistry ecosystem developed through agentic engineering
papers.summary: We describe the vibyverse, developed by agentic engineering, comprising vibe-sketcher for chemical structures and reaction schemes, vibe-qc for electronic-structure calculations, vibe-scheduler for execution and retrieval, vibe-viewer for inspection and presentation, and the Quantum Visualization Format (QVF) for structured exchange. The workflow starts with reaction design in vibe-sketcher, submission through vibe-scheduler, calculation with vibe-qc, and inspection and analysis in vibe-viewer, with scientific data transferred through QVF. We examine the responsibilities of each component and the information that must survive their connections, including charge, multiplicity, geometry, method settings, runtime identity and result provenance. Source inspection identifies implemented interfaces and their compatibility requirements. A Diels–Alder preparation example connects an editable scheme and preoptimized structures to validated QVF and viewer exports. The executed numerical workflow proceeds through MACE geometry optimization, PBE/def2-SVP refinement and DLPNO-CCSD(T) endpoint energies. A proposed water-on-boronnitride example would extend the workflow to periodic structures. The molecular optimization and Hessian use existing PBE routes without an added dispersion correction. Both Hessian stencils identify minima for all three molecules. With an explicit restrictedreference

papers.title: MetaNav: Metacognitive Vision-Language Navigation via Reflective Exploration
papers.summary: Training-free Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) agents powered by foundation models can follow instructions and explore 3D environments. However, existing approaches rely on greedy frontier selection and passive spatial memory, leading to inefficient behaviors such as local oscillation and redundant revisiting. We argue that this stems from a lack of metacognitive capabilities: the agent cannot monitor its exploration progress, diagnose strategy failures, or adapt accordingly. To address this, we propose MetaNav, a metacognitive navigation agent integrating spatial memory, history-aware planning, and reflective correction. Spatial memory builds a persistent 3D semantic map. History-aware planning penalizes revisiting to improve efficiency. Reflective correction detects stagnation and uses an LLM to generate corrective rules that guide future frontier selection. Experiments on GOAT-Bench, HM3D-OVON, and A-EQA show that MetaNav achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing VLM queries by 20.7%, demonstrating that metacognitive reasoning significantly improves robustness and efficiency. The code is available at https://github.com/perfectlxy7/MetaNav.

papers.title: Supporting engagement, behavior change, and equitable self-management in menstrual and menopausal health: A multi-agent digital-health framework
papers.summary: Menstrual-cycle-related conditions and, later, menopausal symptoms are highly prevalent across the female life course and impose a large, under-recognized burden on quality of life and work, yet digital tools to support self-management are fragmented, hard to sustain, and unevenly reached. We propose HERA (Health Engagement and Reflective Agent architecture), a conceptual, hypothesis-generating framework for supporting engagement, behavior change, and equitable self-management in menstrual and menopausal health across the life course. Under human governance, HERA combines two adaptive agents (interpretation and orchestration) with three rule-based modules (self-monitoring and data integration, guidance and content governance, and equity and engagement monitoring) that integrate self-monitoring, deliver personalized feedback, surface governed guidance, monitor equity, and coordinate hand-offs to clinicians and occupational-health services. Distinct from clinician-facing diagnostic agents, HERA is patient-facing and treats equity and engagement as first-class. We distinguish technically feasible from aspirational elements and set out a staged, threshold-gated evaluation plan. HERA is a design reference, not a validated system.

papers.title: XLeaf-Net: an explainable deep learning framework for mango leaf disease classification and severity assessment using Grad-CAM-based visual interpretation
papers.summary: Accurate mango leaf disease recognition is important for automated crop-health assessment, but reliable evaluation requires transparent data partitioning, appropriate baseline comparison, and cautious interpretation of severity and explainability outputs. This study presents XLeaf-Net, an explainable deep-learning framework for mango leaf condition classification, image-derived severity assessment, and Grad-CAM-based visual interpretation. Experiments were conducted on the balanced MangoLeafBD dataset using an image-level stratified train-validation-test protocol with file-level integrity and capture/session-group overlap checks. XLeaf-Net was trained from scratch and compared with from-scratch VGG16, ResNet50, and EfficientNetB0 models under the implemented model-specific training configurations. An auxiliary severity model used conservative, image-derived symptom-intensity proxy labels, while Grad-CAM was applied to qualitatively examine class-discriminative regions. XLeaf-Net achieved 98.67% image-level test accuracy and a 98.66% macro F1-score, outperforming the evaluated from-scratch baselines while using 2.52 million parameters. The severity model achieved 78.17% accuracy and an 80.89% macro F1-score. Grad-CAM visualizations frequently overlapped with visually symptomatic leaf regions in representative correctly classified images. These findings demonstrate strong image-l

papers.title: HITCH: Teaching a Vision-Language Model to Operate a Humanoid through a Whole-Body Harness
papers.summary: Enabling vision-language models (VLMs) to control humanoid robots requires both reliable whole-body interfaces and knowledge of how to use the body that carries over across tasks. We present HITCH (Harness Interfaces To Command Humanoids), a harness in which perception returns the 3D position of any point the VLM selects in its image, and execution turns commands for the pelvis, torso, hands, walking, and gaze into whole-body motion with a learned tracker. We find that both measuring the scene and executing commands accurately raise task success. We then fine-tune a VLM on trajectories in which teacher policies solve five base tasks through HITCH, so that it learns how to operate the humanoid. Without task-specific trajectories, the fine-tuned model completes 51% of SIMPLE episodes and 42.5% of HumanoidArena episodes, and adding five trajectories per SIMPLE task raises its SIMPLE success to 95%. On a real G1, it carries a box and walks to a goal without real training data.

papers.title: Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
papers.summary: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-perf

papers.title: Exploring or Exploiting Generative AI? A Dual-Path, Dual-Horizon Theory of Employee Incremental and Radical Creativity
papers.summary: Recent research has established that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is not a unitary workplace resource: exploratory and exploitative use orientations are associated with different forms of employee creativity, and their value depends on employees' capacity to integrate generated knowledge. This article therefore does not present the basic dual path as a new discovery. Instead, it develops a theoretical integration and dynamic extension that asks why the established paths operate differently, when employees should switch between them, and how short-run augmentation can evolve into either capability accumulation or capability substitution. We distinguish expansive and consolidative modes of knowledge integration, theorize phase-congruent switching rather than static ``high-high'' ambidexterity, and position metacognition as a control mechanism that governs both immediate knowledge conversion and longer-run cognitive development. We further specify cultural tightness and psychological safety as directional boundary conditions and distinguish individual creative gains from collective idea-space diversity. The framework converts emerging empirical regularities into falsifiable propositions about task phase, context, and time, providing a research agenda for sustainable human--AI creativity.

papers.title: Can TDD improve the quality of LLM-migrated code? : A pilot study in an industrial context
papers.summary: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLM) has created new possibilities for automating software development, yet ensuring the quality of AI-generated code remains a major challenge. We aim to investigate if Test-Driven Development (TDD) can improve the quality of code generated by an LLM in a fully autonomous context, within a pilot project at Decerno AB. We added TDD to their pilot workflow, using a design science approach, with continuous refinements to prompt design and workflow structure, based on observed AI behavior. The generated code was evaluated and compared with non-TDD code, using SonarQube for static code analysis. The results indicate that TDD reduced complexity and code duplication, but introduced more quality issues overall, while non-TDD produced fewer, but more severe issues. The generated tests from the TDD workflow focused more on content verification than on behavioral testing, contributing to a lower code coverage per test compared to non-TDD. The findings suggest that TDD involves trade-offs that may favor certain development priorities, in particular where lower complexity and reduced duplication are more beneficial than minimizing total issue count. This indicates that a strict application of TDD may not be optimal in an autonomous AI-driven context, and that exploring more flexible adaptations of the TDD workflow remains interesting for future resea

papers.title: From Coding to Creativity: Integrating Design Thinking into IT and Technology Education
papers.summary: This study examines how the integration of Design Thinking into Information Technology (IT) and technology education can bridge technical programming skills and creative, human-centered problem-solving. Specifically, it explores how the five stages of Design Thinking empathizing, defining, ideating, prototyping, and testing shape students’ creative thinking, active engagement, and collaborative learning experiences. A qualitative research approach was employed, involving teachers, students, and school principals as key informants. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, classroom observations, and documentation of learning activities, then analyzed thematically to identify recurring patterns in teaching practices and student experiences. The findings indicate that Design Thinking creates opportunities for students to move beyond coding procedures toward developing digital solutions that respond to real users’ needs. Through collaborative ideation, iterative prototyping, and feedback-based testing, students demonstrate greater involvement in learning, explore alternative solutions, and communicate their ideas more actively. The approach also provides opportunities to develop empathy, creativity, collaboration, and a willingness to experiment with and revise initial designs. papers.title: Enforcing Narrative Reliability and Epistemic Pacing in LLM-Driven Detective Games via Structured Knowledge Trees
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) enable open-ended dialogue in interactive games, but their non-deterministic outputs make it difficult to preserve authorial control, factual consistency, and the intended sequence of information disclosure. These challenges are particularly significant in detective games, where premature revelation or fabricated details can undermine the logic of player progression. We present a Structured Knowledge Tree architecture coupled with a tri-agent LLM pipeline for controlling dialogue in an open-ended interrogation game. The system separates knowledge retrieval, dialogue generation, and response verification to ensure that the virtual suspect reveals only information permitted by the current narrative state. We evaluate the approach through The Interrogation of Adrian Gale, a playable detective-game testbed, and a formal user study examining hallucination reduction, adherence to authored disclosure sequences, and perceived logical progression. Our results demonstrate that the structured architecture reduces critical hallucinations by 64.78% and entirely prevents premature narrative disclosure. While the strict mechanical constraints introduced usability trade-offs regarding forced conversational reveals, the system successfully enforces rigorous epistemic pacing and provides players with a clear, subjective sense of progression toward solving the case.

papers.title: Solar Photovoltaic Fault Diagnosis: A Comprehensive Survey of Conventional and Machine Learning Techniques
papers.summary: Faults are the principal impediment to achieving elevated levels of efficiency, reliability, and longevity in photovoltaic (PV) systems. In this article, we reviewed solar PV fault diagnostics techniques and compared different fault signature interpretations based on three primary data sources: electrical measurements, environmental conditions, and thermal inspection images. Five overlapping diagnostic perspectives are discussed: measurement modalities (electrical and thermal), statistical methods, optimization-based methods, machine learning techniques. The different approaches are compared regarding: the extent to which faults can be detected; quality of the diagnostic evidence that is generated; what measurements are required for diagnostics; how the topology of the system affects diagnostics; ability to localize faults; under what conditions a diagnosis is validated; and at what time interval the data needs to be acquired. Overall, our evaluation shows there is no single optimal method for identifying faults of all types, primarily because of differences in datasets, definitions of faults, validation conditions and timing measures which make it difficult to make direct comparisons. Finally, we identify areas for future research; Hybrid Physical/Data-Driven Models, Digital Twins, Embedded Inference, Standardized Datasets, Learning with Limited Labels, Longitudinal Field Eval

papers.title: Climate ODER: Information, Coordination, and the Time to Act
papers.summary: An accurate forecast can leave a response team without a usable basis for timely protection. Climate ODER, developed through Observer-Dependent Entropy Retrieval, asks what information must survive, who must retain it, and when it must be secured. In a finite model, available information supports a task when every group of indistinguishable records admits a common acceptable action. As protective options expire, a distinction can become necessary after its last timely recovery opportunity has closed. We establish this separation between preservation and action deadlines. An exact access-locator frontier shows that two initial categories can support timely recovery where immediate action requires arbitrarily many target categories. The recovered answer still carries the target information. A temporal preservation criterion constructs the distinctions that make intermediate recovery operations and final protective choices executable under a specified causal memory mechanism. Extensions give exact criteria for unequal consultation times and a declared class of monotone response rules. For distributed response, we characterize failures of shared-plan selection even when each participant’s information is individually sufficient, construct minimum-cost feature repairs, and derive their budget–deadline frontier under specified acquisition conditions. papers.title: Metacognitive Reasoning in Energy Based Models Using Instance Based Learning Theory
papers.summary: Metacognition involves reasoning about cognitive processes themselves. An example is in resource allocation where we choose how much time and effort to put into a reasoning task before we begin based on our confidence. Current Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems that rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) cannot estimate their uncertainty about an output without first responding, and cannot dynamically allocate resources to producing an output, making this type of metacognitive process difficult. A recently proposed alternative to classic transformer architectures that addresses these two concerns is the Energy Based Model (EBM) which allows for interpretable uncertainty modeling and dynamic allocation of compute resources. While EBMs can allow for control of these two processes, the actual metacognitive task of determining compute allocation based on uncertainty is not directly addressed. Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT) provides an approach to modeling human-like decisions from experience that has previously been applied to predicting human metacognitive reasoning. In this paper we introduce a framework for MEtacognitive Reasoning with Instance-based Learning Theory and Energy Dynamics (MERITED). Grounded in IBLT, this framework allows for control of the computational effort allocated in an EBM to allow for metacognitive control over reasoning effort based on uncertainty

papers.title: Refining collaborative AI literacy: A systematic review of human–AI collaboration competency and AI literacy measures
papers.summary: With the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and its growing role in solving complex problems, human–AI interaction has evolved into a new dimension, where AI is increasingly perceived as a collaborative partner. However, current AI literacy frameworks focus on technical knowledge and ethical use, often neglecting the ability to collaborate effectively with AI as a standalone construct. Conceptualized under the umbrella of AI literacy, the boundaries of human–AI collaboration competency need to be refined in order to create common ground for advancing research and measurement of this essential ability. This systematic review synthesizes 17 studies conducted in higher education settings to examine how human–AI collaboration competency is represented and measured within existing AI literacy scales. The findings reveal that human–AI collaboration is rarely explicitly assessed, let alone as a distinct construct. Some studies included a small number of items that could implicitly refer to collaboration competency or context, but most included no such representation. Drawing on these findings, we propose theoretical implications regarding contexts and factors that should be considered when developing new items, and measurement implications for three possible sub-factors of human–AI collaboration competency: coordination, communication, and metacognition. papers.title: Interactive Digital Media-Assisted SSCS Learning: A Solution to Enhance Problem-Solving Ability and Alleviate Mathematics Anxiety
papers.summary: Problem-solving is a practical skill that students must master in 21st-century learning. However, various findings indicate that this capability remains low among junior high school students, who are beginning to study mathematical concepts in greater depth. Anxiety toward the subject matter, teachers, and mathematics instruction itself is a key factor influencing students' mathematical problem-solving performance. To address this, this study aims to examine the effect of the Search, Solve, Create, and Share (SSCS) learning model, a model that provides a clear roadmap for students to implement Polya's problem-solving steps, assisted by interactive digital media (PhET and Mathigon), on students' problem-solving ability and anxiety. This quasi-experimental study used a factorial design and included eighth-grade students. The research sample was selected using the cluster random sampling technique. Data were collected using a test instrument and a mathematics anxiety questionnaire and were subsequently analyzed using a two-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). The results of the study indicate that: (1) Hypothesis testing showed that there was a significant effect of different learning models on students’ problem-solving ability, with Fobs (= 8.405) > Ftab (= 4.016). papers.title: Leave It Better Than Found: Value-Guided Cooperation in Sequential Tasks
papers.summary: We consider the problem of sequential task continuation, where one robot acts in a workspace that has been affected by a previous robot. Current approaches in multi-robot cooperation rely heavily on co-training or co-optimization, assumingthat the robots have access to collective interaction data during the policy training or planning process. However, as increasingly varied robotic embodiments and policies are deployed and operate in the same real-world environment, learning policies for cooperation becomes infeasible due to the combinatorial explosion of possible robot combinations that need to be accounted for. To address this challenge, this paper considers the problem of ad hoc sequential cooperation between robots that have never before operated together in a shared environment. We demonstrate that robots can explicitly communicate their environmental preferences through sharing their value functions, enabling coordination without the need for prior joint training. To ground this exchange and prevent overconfidence in out-of-distribution states, we further introduce a k-nearest neighbors (KNN)- based uncertainty filter. Our method yields an increase of up to 48.5 pp compared with naive or even selfish agents, in task success rates across simulated and real-world experiments, demonstrating that value function transmission between agents is useful not merely as an internal

papers.title: Should You Split Decode? Disaggregation Across Future Models and Accelerators
papers.summary: For large language model (LLM) inference, prefill/decode disaggregation (P/D) is deployed in production to isolate phases with different resource demands. Attention/feed-forward network disaggregation (AFD) splits decode again, but adds communication, placement constraints, and another provisioned pool. We ask whether role-specific placement repays this cost as models and accelerator roadmaps change. Infrastructure is committed before future models and hardware can be benchmarked. We present SiliconForge, a calibrated model that varies the serving decomposition and hardware assignment independently. We compare P/D and P/D+AFD across four model directions, four accelerator classes anchored to current and announced parts, and two fabrics. We co-optimize each design using the same rules for pipeline overlap and the same power budget. Our main comparisons show no robust deployment-level AFD advantage in service-level objective (SLO) goodput per kW. Most nominal estimates favor P/D. The largest AFD lead comes from fitting one more prefill replica, not from a more efficient decode pool. AFD has a nominal lead in the KV-heavy (key-value) model direction when the co-located expert pool spans several small scale-up domains. Larger domains or a fast fabric for both designs weaken that lead. We therefore find that prefill provisioning, decode memory bandwidth, links, and pool granularity

papers.title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
papers.summary: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent game

papers.title: An Assessment of Accessibility and Affordability of Inpatient Psychiatric Care in Tennessee
papers.summary: Introduction: Access to mental health has seen changes over the past decade, but little research and attention have been given to access to inpatient psychiatric facilities. Inpatient psychiatric care is crucial for patients experiencing mental health emergencies who need immediate access to care. Gaps in spatial accessibility, affordability, and the access and assessment process were identified due to a lack of available information in the field. Methods: Secondary data from the Tennessee Department of Health were used to assess financial accessibility through payer source charges and patient encounters, as well as through mapping of inpatient psychiatric facilities and conducting drive time and coverage area analyses. Primary data were collected through interviews with clinicians located in Northeastern Tennessee to gain insight into the assessment process and gather their perceptions of inpatient care. Results: Longitudinal descriptive reviews on the financial accessibility among Tennessee Inpatient Facilities. This showed increased variability among facilities when stratified by region, ownership, and type of operation. Spatial accessibility in ArcGIS showed 82% of counties were not covered within a 30-minute radius of inpatient facilities. Analysis showed that Middle Tennessee had significantly less coverage from inpatient facilities and raised concerns about spatial-socia

papers.title: Pieces Solving a Puzzle: Emerging Roles and Cross-Field Analogies During a Distributed Epistemic Game
papers.summary: In an effort to describe why some problems can’t be solved, a character compared them to a cubic meter of platinum - a block so dense that all the people who could squeeze around it still couldn’t lift it off the ground. In the same way, these problems simply can’t have enough people gathered around and communicating about them - and so they remain unsolved. This research looks at the first Polymath Project (2009) as an example of a distributed epistemic game to examine how groups engage with complex problems. and without a locally omniscient individual. In this setting of epistemic uncertainty, interactions between individuals reveal patterns of participation, and an analogy opens a new solution pathway by introducing a problem-solving approach from another field. These insights answer the initial question of the Polymath Project - ‘Is massively collaborative mathematics possible?’ - and offer hope for lifting the cubic meter of other unsolvable problems.

papers.title: Designing a Curriculum Model Based on Artificial Intelligence and Purposeful Physical Activity to Enhance Learning Self-Regulation, Mental Health, and Psychological Well-Being among Students
papers.summary: Objective: The objective of this study was to design and validate a curriculum model based on artificial intelligence and purposeful physical activity with emphasis on enhancing learning self-regulation, mental health, and psychological well-being among students. Methods and Materials: This applied developmental study was conducted using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. In the qualitative phase, 20 experts in curriculum studies, educational technology, artificial intelligence in education, physical education, educational psychology, and student mental health were selected through purposive criterion-based sampling from Tehran and participated in semi-structured interviews. The interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis to extract the main dimensions, components, and indicators of the proposed curriculum model. Data were collected using a researcher-made curriculum model validation questionnaire, a learning self-regulation questionnaire, the General Health Questionnaire, and a psychological well-being scale. papers.title: DSLE: A Learning Environment for Dark Souls Boss Encounters
papers.summary: We introduce the Dark Souls Learning Environment (DSLE), a containerized platform that presents all 22 boss encounters of Dark Souls: Remastered as game-playing agent benchmarks through a Gymnasium-style interface. DSLE combines real-time combat, high-dimensional visual input, and sparse terminal rewards, with each environment step being a real action executed against the running game. To support controlled comparison, we define DSLE-5, a representative five-boss subset, spanning a melee fight, a spatially constrained arena, an environmental-hazard fight, a multi-target fight, and a fast final-boss fight, that we recommend as the starting suite for agents built on DSLE. On DSLE-5 we evaluate a random policy, an expert system, an evolutionary baseline, and PPO and DQN agents trained from visual input. The expert system and the evolutionary baseline each defeat the Asylum Demon, the game's tutorial boss (63% and 43% peak win rates), but none of the five methods defeats the other four DSLE-5 bosses; PPO and DQN show no measurable learning (at most 0.33% win rate on the tutorial boss, 0% elsewhere) within a budget that already costs tens of wall-clock hours per run. A broader study running the evolutionary baseline across all 22 encounters under advantaged all level-50 stats yields wins on only a handful of additional early-game bosses and leaves the rest unwon.
